questions.enonce_markdown: Explain how the information encoded in DNA is used to make protein. *[12 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Overview.** The sequence of nucleotides in a gene is a code for the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The code is a **triplet code**: three bases on DNA (a triplet) specify one amino acid. It is **degenerate** (most amino acids have more than one codon), **non-overlapping** and **almost universal**. Protein synthesis has two stages, **transcription** (in the nucleus) and **translation** (at the ribosomes in the cytoplasm).

**1. Transcription (DNA to messenger RNA)**

- The enzyme **RNA polymerase** binds to the **promoter** region at the start of the gene. The DNA double helix unwinds locally and the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs break, exposing the bases of the **template (antisense) strand**.
- Free **RNA nucleotides** from the nucleoplasm pair with the exposed bases by complementary base pairing: A with U, T with A, G with C, C with G. (Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.)
- RNA polymerase joins the nucleotides by **phosphodiester bonds** and moves along the gene in the $5' \to 3'$ direction, making a single-stranded molecule of **messenger RNA (mRNA)**. The DNA re-forms the double helix behind it.
- At a **terminator** sequence, transcription stops and the primary transcript is released.
- In eukaryotes the primary transcript (pre-mRNA) is **processed**: the non-coding **introns** are removed and the coding **exons** are spliced together; a **cap** is added at the $5'$ end and a **poly-A tail** at the $3'$ end. The mature mRNA leaves the nucleus through a **nuclear pore** and enters the cytoplasm.

**2. Translation (mRNA to polypeptide)**

- **Activation of amino acids.** In the cytoplasm each amino acid is joined to its own **transfer RNA (tRNA)** by a specific enzyme (aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase), using energy from **ATP**. Each tRNA has an **anticodon** (three bases) complementary to the codon of that amino acid.
- **Initiation.** The small ribosomal subunit binds to the mRNA and moves to the **start codon AUG**. The first tRNA, carrying methionine, pairs with it through its anticodon UAC. The large subunit then joins, forming a complete **ribosome** with the tRNA in the P site.
- **Elongation.** A second tRNA, whose anticodon is complementary to the next codon, enters the A site. The enzyme **peptidyl transferase** forms a **peptide bond** between the two amino acids, so the polypeptide is passed to the tRNA in the A site. The ribosome then moves along the mRNA by **one codon (translocation)**; the empty tRNA leaves and returns to the cytoplasm to pick up another amino acid. The cycle is repeated, adding one amino acid at a time and lengthening the chain.
- **Termination.** When a **stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA)** reaches the A site, no tRNA matches it; a **release factor** binds, the polypeptide is released and the ribosome subunits separate.
- Many ribosomes read the same mRNA at once (a **polyribosome** or polysome), so many copies of the polypeptide are made quickly. The polypeptide then folds (secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure) and may be modified in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus.

**Worked example of the information flow**

| DNA template triplet | mRNA codon | tRNA anticodon | Amino acid |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAC | AUG | UAC | methionine (start) |
| AAA | UUU | AAA | phenylalanine |
| ACT | UGA | none | stop |

**Diagram expected (optional but rewarded).** Draw a short stretch of DNA with the template strand, the mRNA copy being made with RNA polymerase labelled, and a ribosome on the mRNA with two tRNA molecules (anticodon, amino acid, peptide bond, growing polypeptide, direction of movement labelled).

questions.enonce_markdown: How is the synthesis of proteins regulated by enzyme induction and enzyme repression? *[8 marks]* *(12, 8 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Cells make a protein only when it is needed. In bacteria, groups of genes are controlled together as an **operon** (the model of **Jacob and Monod**). An operon has: a **regulator gene** (makes a repressor protein), a **promoter** (where RNA polymerase binds), an **operator** (where the repressor binds) and the **structural genes** coding for the enzymes.

**1. Enzyme induction - the lac operon of *Escherichia coli* (an inducible system)**

An **inducible enzyme** is made only when its substrate (the **inducer**) is present, e.g. the enzymes that digest lactose.

- *Lactose absent:* the regulator gene (lacI) makes an active **repressor protein**. It binds to the **operator** and blocks the promoter, so RNA polymerase cannot transcribe the structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA). The genes are **switched off**: no enzyme is made, which saves energy.
- *Lactose present:* a derivative of lactose (allolactose) acts as the **inducer**. It binds to the repressor at its allosteric site and changes its shape, so the repressor can no longer bind to the operator. RNA polymerase moves along and transcribes the structural genes. The enzymes **beta-galactosidase** (splits lactose into glucose and galactose), **permease** and **transacetylase** are made: the genes are **switched on**.
- When all the lactose has been used, the repressor binds again to the operator and the enzymes are no longer made.

**2. Enzyme repression - the trp operon (a repressible system)**

A **repressible enzyme** is made all the time until the **end product** of the pathway builds up.

- *Tryptophan low:* the repressor made by the regulator gene is **inactive** (it cannot bind to the operator). RNA polymerase transcribes the genes and the enzymes that synthesise tryptophan are made.
- *Tryptophan high:* tryptophan acts as a **co-repressor**. It binds to the repressor and makes it **active**; the repressor-tryptophan complex binds to the operator and **blocks transcription**. The enzymes are no longer made and no more tryptophan is produced.

**Significance.** Both mechanisms are forms of **negative feedback at the level of gene expression**: the cell makes enzymes only when they are useful (induction) and stops making them when the product is plentiful (repression), so amino acids and energy are not wasted.
